PROJECT PLAN

Description

A project plan includes taking the results of other planning processes and placing them
into a consistent document.

Purpose

A project plan is a document used to coordinate all project planning documents and help
guide a project’s execution and control. Project plans also document project planning
assumptions and decisions and regarding choices, facilitate communication among
stakeholders, define the content, extent, and timing of key management reviews, and
provide a baseline for progress measurement and project control.

Participants

Since information is required from all of the project management knowledge areas.
Working with the project team and other stakeholders to create a project plan will help
the project manager guide the project’s execution and understand the overall project.

Timing

A project plan is the first process of project integration management. Project plans should
be dynamic, flexible and subject to change when the environment or project changes.

Techniques

the project manager guide the project’s execution and understand the overall project.

A project plan is the first process of project integration management. Project plans should
be dynamic, flexible and subject to change when the environment or project changes.

Techniques

Just as projects are unique, so are project plans. A small project concerning a few people
over a couple of months might have a project plan consisting of only a project charter,
scope statement, and Gantt chart. A large project concerning a hundred people over three
years would have a great deal more detailed project plan. It is important to adapt a project
plan to fit the needs of specific projects. The project plan should guide the work, so they
should be only as detailed as needed for each project.
There are however, common elements to most project plans. Parts of project plan include
and introduction or overview of the project, a description of how the project is organized,
the management and technical processes used on the project, and sections describing the
work to be performed, the schedule, and the budget.

gain insights into your own learning journey;

consider the impact of your learning on real-world scenarios; and

A2=Purpose - This Risk Log provides a place to document identified risks and record the analysis undertaken on them
A3=There are three approaches to assessing risk in procurement evaluation. Tenders that are over $10m in value and  have low margins in their business case or are immature markets/technology (complex), should have an full Quanitative Risk analysis undertaken to quantify the risks. 
Tenders that are more than $100k and less than $10m (Moderate) should undertake a process to quantify the cost of treatments and take those costs into consideration of the Financial Analysis Model used for the evaluation.  
Tenders that are less than $100k (Simple) may undertake a quantitative process that equates to a factor that can be applied to the VFM scores.
A4=There are generally 5 Critical Success Factors associated with the analysis of risk events. These are: 
- Price / Commercial risk (such as financial viability)
- Schedule
- Quality or ability to complete the scope of work
- Safety
- Reputation
A5=The model allows some or all of these critical success factors to be considered in the risk evaluation. The user may nominate a weighting for each of these critical success factors. The weightings used relate across the CSFs and does not impact on the overall risk score or risk factor. The numerical value of the waiting is shown adjacent to the critical success factor.

Description

Design Specification is a set of rules intended to define the design deliverables and guide
the design process of a particular development project.

Purpose

The Design Specification manuals purpose is to guide the development process. Team
members provide document, maintain a disciplined approach to process, performance,
simplicity, and clarity to reduced common errors in document report.

Participations

The Design Specification will need to be done by a group member that will be overseeing
the process of design, preferable with the experience in both software development and
object-orientated development. This chosen person(s) will take care of all the Design
Specification in the documents of the reports.

Timing

The Design Specification must be completed in the beginning of project.

Technique

Borrow some existing project (Design Specification) from other organizations.

Rubin, S K. (1997), Developing Object-Oriented Software: an experience-based approach,

Starter team roles – Guidance Notes
How to use these role descriptions
These roles are a starting point, not a fixed structure. Every project is different, and your team should adapt the roles to suit your project, sponsor, mentor, team size, and final outputs.
In a small team, one person may hold more than one role, and some roles may be shared. The key point is that your team agrees who is accountable for each responsibility. Accountable means making sure the work is planned, followed up, completed, and recorded - not necessarily doing all the work yourself.
Teams should review their roles regularly, especially if the project changes direction. Pay particular attention to basic project management tasks that are easy to miss, including recording decisions, tracking scope changes, sending minutes, managing issues and risks, and checking progress against the timeline.
A useful test is:
A useful test is: when something needs to be done, does the team know who is responsible for making sure it does not get dropped? If something goes wrong, do we know who was responsible for making sure it was followed up?
A role is useful only if it helps the team communicate, make decisions, and deliver the project more effectively.

Observe

You have already been in a bunch of meetings, what did you see?

Strategise:

How does the sponsor meeting fit - what role does it play?

 • How will the world be a little better after the visit?

Plan/design:

Work out a sort of meeting script that will cover the topics in a logical order:

 • Determine the materials you'll provide – early thoughts, progress reports in

 • Make sure everyone has mobile numbers in case of problems.

Develop/test:

Prepare all the necessary materials and walk through the meeting in situ.

Act :

Contact each participant, send agenda and materials, put meeting into their diaries.

 • Meet and greet on the day - see the hints from your research (above)
 • Stick to the allocated time – don’t be late and don’t run over time.

Follow-up and review:

 • Write up notes of the meeting, decisions and actions allocated to specific
 people. Send the participants a short note of thanks for their time and their
 input, and ask for corrections to the notes you have taken.

 • Specify what you'll do better next time (e. g. in your weekly reflection)

Marking criteria (rubric), group presentation

 Good presentations relay relevant information, tailored to your audience, and
 require you to engage your audience.

 Marking criteria for your group project reflect this:

  Clarity and coherence
  Flow of information
  Innovative, creative, captivating and impressive approach
  Teamwork at presentation
  Engagement with the panel (audience) including Q&A.

 Keep the rubric in mind when creating your presentation!

Presentation skills

Presentation skills are learned and developed through experience.
Like most skills, presentation skills include a range of ‘sub’ skills, e.g.:

• Visual Communication • Managing emotions
• Interpersonal Communication • Self-awareness
• Verbal Communication • Leadership
• Humour • Focus on the audience
• Storytelling • Active listening
• Attracting the audience • Time management
• Keeping things simple • Research
• Using body language
• Communicating succinctly
• Explaining specialist content in a way that people without that knowledge can understand

How to approach creating your presentation

 Assume your audience doesn’t know you or that you’re doing this
 presentation as part of your unit
 (so: introduce yourself and why you are presenting!)
 Consider the purpose of your presentation: as part of your unit, it is to
 develop a range of knowledge and skills
 (so: it’s ok if things went wrong / you didn’t get the results you hoped
 for / you didn’t get any results –
 focus on what you did / learned / how you responded to challenges &
 found solutions)
 Consider the main points you want to get across. You can’t fit everything
 in your presentation.
 Consider the logical flow of information with equal weight to beginning,
 middle and end
 Assume your audience has knowledge in your field, but consider defining
 / explaining certain concepts
 Use everyday language, keep your sentences short

 Practice!

Visual aids

 Visual aids include images, videos, colours, graphs & tables, etc.
 When including visual aids, consider that visual aids should aim to:
  support your words, i.e., to clarify important points
  enhance engagement

 Considering the purpose of your visual aid can then help you to:
  Choose the appropriate visual aid, e.g., photo, table, graph, colour,
 font, highlight
  Assess whether your visual aid supports the point you’re making, or
 distracts from the presentation

 Make sure that your visual aid does not replace you, the speaker.

Poster presentations

 Posters should:
 • cover all main points that you would discuss in a presentation.
 • have creative and artistic presentation and design
 • be clear, succinct, intuitive, comprehensive and self-explanatory.

 Similar to verbal presentations, consider your:
 content, design, words to present, including how you tell your story and body
 language.

Practically

 A research poster is meant to be a very brief overview of your project with only
 highlights and summary information. Your aim is to:

 Catch the attention of your audience
  think of your layout and visuals

 You want them to stop and read your information in a minute or so
  Include limited information only

 You then want them to ask questions / have a further discussion about your topic
  Avoid reading information off your poster –
 you can offer a handout with further details
  Research your audience: can you make a link between your project and what
 your audience is interested in?

Designing your poster

Meet the design aims of your poster presentation by:

• Having a short title, drawing interest
• Information needs to be grouped in sections, with words mixed with tables,
 graphs.
• Important information should be legible from about 2-3 metres away
• Text is clear and to the point
• Use dot points, numbering, and headlines to make it easy to read
• Consider appropriate use of graphics, colours (contrast) and simple fonts
• Consistent and clean layout, use bold and font side sparingly
• Include your name, institutional affiliation, and acknowledgments
Keep it simple, with about 40% blank space!

Work breakdown structure (WBS)
Timing — prepared during the scope definition process, to define further the work required for the 
project and break it down into manageable pieces
Technique — Approaches for developing a WBS include:
 Using guidelines: some organizations provide guidelines and templates for developing work 
breakdown structures. It is important to follow them.
 The analogy approach: use a similar project’s WBS as a starting point.
 The top-down approach: team members start with the largest items of the project and break them 
into their subordinate items. This process involves refining the work into greater and greater levels 
of detail.
 The bottom-up approach: team members first identify as many specific tasks related to the project 
as possible. They then aggregate the specific tasks and organize them into summary activities, or 
higher levels in the WBS.
 The mind-mapping approach: a technique that uses branches radiating out from a core idea to 
structure thoughts and ideas. Instead of writing down tasks in a list or immediately trying to create a 
structure for tasks, mind mapping allow people to write and even draw pictures of ideas in a non-
linear format.

Who are the stakeholders of a project ? 
List the stakeholders of your own project

- Knowing them who they are important 
• Stakeholders are the people and organisations involved in, or 
impacted by, the intervention/ project
• They include diverse groups such as customers, sponsors, 
impacted management, impacted staff, external organisations 
and even the public or the press
• Stakeholders can positively or negatively impact the project, so it 
is important to understand their interests and managed them to 
increase the chance of project success
• Project team and the project sponsor are also stakeholders, but require different 
management to stakeholders who are not on the project team
• Project sponsor is the most critical stakeholder. They need to be positive towards the 
project, as they gain most from the outcomes
STAKEHOLDER IDENTIFICATION

Stakeholders analysis
• Positive stakeholders can be leveraged to enhance 
project success and negative stakeholders need to be 
encouraged to support the project, or at least be 
neutral in their impact
• Use three-step process outlined in the PMBoK:
– Step 1: identify all potential project stakeholders
– Step 2: analyse the potential impact of each stakeholder
– Step 3: assess likely stakeholder reactions and plan to get support
Source: PMI, 2013,

interest in the service
 Stakeholder ownership of the objective

 Safety issues and Hazards
 New or immature design concepts
 Novel or emerging technology
 High level of system integration required
 Low level of project resourcing
 External dependencies on other projects
 Constraints on access to Intellectual Property
 Low availability of capable subcontractors
 Extensive safety critical/mission critical requirements
 High systems integration effort required
 Test and acceptance plans not established early

 Academic content

 Unit description

 In the Technology Capstone Project unit, students are exposed to complex real-life problems proposed in
 collaboration with diverse stakeholders, which they solve in a collaborative group setting, utilising their
 technical, research, innovation, and project management skills under the guidance of a mentor and project
 sponsor. Students will work on a technology focused research project in a team. The projects will enable
 students to develop their theoretical knowledge further in an area of interest. Through critical analysis, thesis
 of research findings and problem-solving, the students will be able to apply their knowledge in a unique
 context to understand how research could improve and advance the body of knowledge related to technology.
 Students' engagement with the latest technology and industry practices using experiential learning approach,
 improves their understanding of their future profession, and develops their skills and competencies to be more
 effective in future workplaces.

 After successful completion of this unit, students will be able to:

 1. Synthesise a complex problem from multi-dimensional, socio technical and socio-economic perspectives in

 1. Synthesise a complex problem from multi-dimensional, socio technical and socio-economic perspectives in

 2. Use research and projects management methodologies to collaboratively solve complex problems with due
 consideration to diverse groups including indigenous communities;

 3. Use appropriate research tools, resources and technologies;

 4. Critically evaluate and apply suitable different qualitative and quantitative methods in research; and

 5. Synthesise and disseminate research and project outcomes to diverse audiences.

 negotiate, and resolve conflict

This unit addresses complex computing problems that have one or more of the following characteristics:

 - involves wide-ranging or conflicting technical, computing, and other issues;

 - has no obvious solution, and requires conceptual thinking and innovative analysis to formulate suitable
 abstract models;

 - a solution requires the use of in-depth computing or domain knowledge and an analytical approach that is
 based on well-founded principles;

 - involves infrequently encountered issues;

 - is outside problems encompassed by standards and standard practice for professional computing;

 - involves diverse groups of stakeholders with widely varying needs;

 - has significant consequences in a range of contexts;

 - is a high-level problem possibly including many component parts or sub-problems;

 - identification of a requirement or the cause of a problem is ill defined or unknown.

 1C Peer evaluation

 Introduction

 Peer evaluation is an important component of group assessment. The objective is to ensure fairness which will
 reflect the participation and contribution of each student in the group project. As a project manager you must
 manage and evaluate the performances of your team members, which is critical to manage human assets
 efficiently. Group dynamics amongst the project members is a complex issue, which plays an important role in
 the project outcome. In a real-life situation, you'll have to work with project teams of diverse team members
 with different personalities. Finally, the two aspects of learning outcome or assignment, i.e., Product (what is
 the answer/ deliverables) and the second one is Process (how you do/achieve it) are equally important. While
 the assessor will mark the product/report, the process part will be largely reflected through your peer
 evaluation so that it can accurately reflect individual contributions.

 Process

 Peer evaluation will be administered using a well-designed questionnaire consisting of 10 items (each with a
 range of 1-10 scale). The aggregated mean of peer evaluation of an individual member will be the determinant
 of individual marks for the project report. For example, if a student obtains 80% in peer evaluation, that means
 he/she will get 80% of the total marks obtained by the group for the report. If anyone fails to submit the peer
 evaluation or submits an unconstructive/ casual submission (which is almost like submitting a blank paper in
 the exam) undermining the spirit of this peer evaluation he/she will not only miss the 3% allotted mark for peer
 evaluation, also his/her evaluation paper will not be calculated to determine the average. By doing this, the
 student will miss the opportunity to have his/her valuable input to the evaluation process. If the evaluation is
 done diligently, everyone in the group is not supposed to get equal marks in every item of this survey, as the
 items capture various aspects of team participation and individual attributes.

 Note : Average percentage score, i.e. peer evaluation index (PEI) will be used to obtain individual score for
 final group assignment. To recognise both the team efforts and individual contributions of the final group
 assignments, only 50% of the final group assignment mark (E1+E2+E3) will be moderated by the PEI.

 PEI = Average Peer Evaluation/Max Average Peer Evaluation in Group

 FAQs about delivery and project arrangements

 1 Can this unit be attended or completed online?
 Capstone project units are not ideal or appropriate for online delivery and can be challenging to complete entirely
 online. If this is the last unit required for a degree, or there are other compelling reasons, enrolment may be possible
 with permission. Exceptional online participation was permitted during the pandemic. A case will be considered only

 2 Why is online delivery not recommended when real projects can operate remotely?
 Special permission is required for online participation. Capstone objectives and learning outcomes are not always
 well suited to online delivery. Projects come from industry and academic sponsors, and some require physical
 interaction, laboratory access or other resources. Sponsors may be reluctant to support projects without physical
 interaction. Projects include physical artefacts and information systems research to accommodate diverse interests
 and expertise. Feedback from previous semesters indicated that students and sponsors preferred face-to-face
 project environments for the experience and to reduce misunderstandings.

 3 Can a project from my workplace be used as a capstone project?
 It may be possible, but the proposal must come from a sponsor or academic supervisor. The usual process is for
 convenors to invite project proposals from potential sponsors and supervisors, after which students choose from the
 resulting list. A willing sponsor or supervisor is needed, and the project must meet the unit outline criteria. If an
 industry sponsor is interested, send the sponsor's email address and project details to the convenors so they can
 send an invitation. All group members, normally three or four, must agree to select and work on the project.

 4 Can students from different units work in the same team or project?
 No. The ITS Capstone units are 9785 (undergraduate) and 11522 (postgraduate). Mixing students from different
 units in the same team or project creates assessment difficulties.

 5 Can the team choose its programming language?
 The sponsor and supervisor decide. Some sponsors mandate a technical platform and language; others welcome
 team recommendations. Check with sponsors and supervisors when choosing projects.

 6 What if none of our selected projects can be allocated to our group?
 Each team must nominate three project choices. If all three are unavailable, resubmit the expression of interest
 (EOI) with new choices and consult the convenors about further options.

 7 Is project allocation first come first served when two teams choose the same project?
 No. Allocation considers factors including students being in the same unit, a suitable team size, matching skills,
 sponsor preferences and submission order. If all other factors are equal, the team that submitted first is more likely
 to receive the project.

Unit Assessments Summary

Engagement &
 Participation (10%)

+ Marks awarded to each team member
 individually by the sponsor/mentor
+ No submission required
+ Factors such as meeting attendance and
 participation, email communication, sponsor
 feedback, etc., will be considered

Final Assessment Individual
Marks Calculation

+ The group marks are individualised based on
 the peer evaluation index (PEI)
+ PEI is calculated based on the peer
 evaluation submitted by all the team
 members
+ Final individual mark (out of 55) will be
 calculated as
 Individual Mark = (Poster + Presentation +
 Report) / 2 + (PEI * (Poster + Presentation +
 Report) / 2)

Peer Evaluation (3%)

+ 3 marks for submitting a valid peer evaluation
 (invalid submissions will get a 0, there’s no in-
 between)
+ 10 criteria for each team member (including self ),
 with a score ranging from 0-10 for each criterion
+ Maximum total marks you can give for each team
 member is 100
+ The Peer Evaluation Index (PEI) is a value between
 0 and 1, calculated using the average of the marks
 given by all team members (including self ) for
 each member out of 100, dividing it by the highest
 average among the team members (see next slide)

PEI Calculation –
Steps

+ Step 1 – The average peer evaluation score (out of
 100) for each team member, including their self-
 evaluation, is taken
+ Step 2 – The average of each team member is
 divided by the highest peer evaluation average
 scored by a member on the team
 This means that the team member with the highest
 average will get the same individual mark as the
 group mark, and the others will get slightly less

PEI Calculation -
Example

+ Assume there is a group of 4 students – A , B , C &
 D, with average peer evaluation scores of 80, 90,
 95 & 85
+ The highest average in the group is 95, which is C’s
 PEI of A = 80/95 = 0.84, of B = 90/95 = 0.95, of C =
 95/95 = 1, of D = 85/95 = 0.89
 The PEI will then be multiplied with half of the total
 group mark out of 55 and added to half of the
 total group mark to get the individual mark out of
 55

Peer Evaluation -
Guidelines

+ Include a self-evaluation in addition to evaluating
 your team members
+ For a peer evaluation to be valid, there should be a
 difference in the scores given to each team
 member
+ Giving 10 for all criteria for everyone is N OT a
 valid peer evaluation, it just means you lose 3
 marks, and your evaluation will not be considered
 in calculating the peer evaluation index (PEI)
+ Further enquiries might be made into teams where
 there is a large discrepancy in the peer evaluation
 marks given for a team member by their
 teammates

Peer Evaluation –
Guidelines (contd.)

+ To make the process easy, try to identify which team
 member (might be yourself ) performed the best for
 each of the 10 criteria and give them a high score
 (close to 10, preferably not 10)
+ Compare the other team members’ performances to
 that and give them slightly lower scores for that
 criterion
+ Repeat the process* for all 10 criteria and add
 everyone’s scores up, and voila, you have a valid
 peer evaluation!
 *This is just a general tip and doesn’t need to be
 strictly followed, but whatever approach you take,
 make sure you’re applying the same standards
 consistently for all team members

Peer Evaluation –
Guidelines (contd.)

+ Be honest and fair in your evaluation of yourself
 and your team members in accordance with the
 ACS code of ethics
 If a team member (including yourself ) has made
 good contributions, don’t unnecessarily reduce
 their marks
 If a team member (including yourself ) has not
 contributed, don’t give them unreasonably high
 marks
+ The peer evaluation is confidential
 Your teammates won’t know what marks you gave
 them unless you tell them (hint: shh, don’t tell
 them!)

Poster (15%)

+ Follow the tips and guidelines provided

 The journal develops critical thinking and personal reflection on lectures, workshops and the group project.
 It supports insights into the student’s learning journey, application of course concepts to the project,
 consideration of future project or professional practice, and understanding of broader real-life IT impacts on
 society, organisations and ethics.

 This weekly journal is not a group project log. Focus on individual engagement, personal contributions,
 reflections on team processes and learning from course content.

 5. Content required in each entry

 Significant individual experience: Describe a significant aspect of your week from lectures, guest
 lectures, tutorials or the group project. Examples include research, software testing, planning and running
 sponsor or mentor meetings, or another noteworthy project experience.

 Personal action and learning: Explain what you personally did, what you learnt, and how a project
 management principle or technique was applied or could have been applied more effectively.

 Ethical consideration: Describe any ethical consideration or dilemma faced. Examples include decisions
 under uncertainty, fairness in task allocation, handling client or team expectations, data security and
 professional integrity.

 Reflection and future application: Reflect on the experience, the actions you personally took, what you
 learnt and how you can apply the insight to the project in coming weeks.

Rubric: communication and presentation

 8.2 Communication and presentation | 5 points

 HD | 5 to >4.28 Pts

 Excellent grammar and spelling with superior sentence, paragraph, and overall structure. Uses language
 that is precise and engaging, with notable sense of voice, and awareness of purpose. Demonstrates
 control of the conventions with essentially no errors, even with sophisticated language.

 DI | 4.28 to >3.78 Pts

 Very good grammar and spelling with very good sentence, paragraph, and overall structure. Uses
 language that is fluent and original, with evident sense of voice, and awareness of purpose. Demonstrates
 control of the conventions, exhibiting occasional errors only when using sophisticated language.

 Cr | 3.78 to >3.28 Pts

 Sound grammar, spelling, and structure but in need of some improvement. Uses basic but appropriate
 language, with a basic sense of voice, some awareness of purpose. Demonstrates partial control of the
 conventions, exhibiting occasional errors that do not hinder comprehension.

 P | 3.28 to >2.5 Pts

 Adequate grammar, spelling, and structure, but in need of significant improvement. Uses language that is
 vague or imprecise for the purpose, with little sense of voice. Demonstrates limited control of the
 conventions, exhibiting frequent errors that make comprehension difficult.

 Fail | 2.5 to >0 Pts

 Poor grammar and spelling and illogical and incoherent structure. Uses language that is unsuitable for the
 purpose. Demonstrates little or no control of the conventions, making comprehension almost impossible.
